stories.title: NASA's Swift Observatory burned up over Indonesia after nearly 22 years in orbit
paragraphs: NASA said the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered at 7:39 a.m. EST on Nov. 4, 2026, over North Sumatra, Indonesia. Live Science reports the roughly 3,200-pound spacecraft was expected mostly to burn up, with a 1-in-2,100 chance of debris reaching a populated area, and no damage or injuries reported.

The Conversation says Swift launched in 2004 to chase gamma-ray bursts and other fast events with three telescopes, and could slew about 50 degrees in under 75 seconds. By 2015 it had logged its 1,000th gamma-ray burst; NASA estimates about 7,000 related research papers.

Solar-maximum drag and a failed July 2026 Katalyst Space Technologies boost mission left Swift on a path to reentry, according to both outlets. Swift also aided supernova alerts, IceCube neutrino localization, and a 2025 hydroxyl detection on 3I/ATLAS.

image.credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab, via Live Science

stories.title: SLAC-led team confirms altermagnetism as a third magnetic phase
paragraphs: ScienceDaily reports that a SLAC-led team published in Science experimental confirmation of altermagnetism in manganese telluride (MnTe). Lead author Daniel Jost said the results provide robust confirmation that this third phase is real. The Science paper is dated Oct. 29, 2026.

According to SLAC, altermagnets combine antiferromagnet-like alternating spins with a rotated crystal environment around opposite spins—a symmetry break proposed in 2022. Using circularly polarized X-rays at ESRF's ID32 beamline, the team measured a chiral scattering difference between left- and right-handed light that conventional antiferromagnets should not show.

Jost said altermagnets offer zero net magnetization for stability plus spin-polarized currents that are useful for reading information in spintronic devices. The DOE Office of Science partly funded the work.

image.credit: Greg Stewart/SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, via ScienceDaily
image.alt: Graphic comparing three forms of magnetism

stories.title: Record-low temperature created with ultracold atoms on China's Tiangong station
paragraphs: Science News reports that researchers cooled about 20,000 rubidium atoms on China's Tiangong space station to roughly 10 picokelvins, forming a Bose-Einstein condensate colder than any previously reported. The study appears in Science on Nov. 5, 2026.

Laser traps slowed the atoms in microgravity, avoiding the sagging gravity causes on Earth. Earlier ISS condensates reached about 52 picokelvins, and a drop-tower experiment reached 38 picokelvins; orbital free fall lasts far longer than a tower drop.
Science News says such ultracold atoms help probe exotic quantum states and tests of the equivalence principle.

stories.title: Voyager 1 resumes contact after a 48-hour communications pause
paragraphs: JPL said NASA's Deep Space Network lost Voyager 1's signal on Oct. 18–19, 2026, then regained it on Oct. 20 after about 48 hours, before troubleshooting commands could arrive. Space.com notes the probe is nearly one light-day from Earth and will hit that distance on Nov. 18.

Engineers found one thruster group went offline and backups engaged automatically under fault protection. Mission manager Kareem Badaruddin called it the first time the spacecraft has behaved this way. The root cause remains under investigation.

In early September, JPL finished Voyager 1's "Big Bang" power swap—replacing three devices with lower-power alternatives—after a similar change on Voyager 2 about six weeks earlier, aiming to keep remaining science instruments running longer as each craft loses about 4 watts of power per year.
